NEW MAYORS

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
what does the future hold for SA with coalition governments taking control in 4 of the country's major cities?

Summary:
While the ANC is still the country's ruling party - they've lost power in 4 of the 6 major cities in SA - with Tshwane & Johannesburg falling under two DA mayors.

What does the mean for the country? How will these coalitions work? And these two new mayor's the right candidates - they promise change - but how will it be delivered?


Further information:
South Africans are overestimating the “good news” of the DA, EFF and smaller parties ganging up against the ANC, as the political and economic realities in South Africa have just become far more complex.

This is according to Nomura chief strategist for Africa, Peter Attard Montalto, who has provided a breakdown of the coalitions formed over the past few days, and a number of implications for investors looking to put money into the country.

Coming out of the coalition talks, The DA looks set to gain mayorship and a degree of control in major metros in the country – metros which control 85% of the municipal finance budget in South Africa.

This includes outright control of the City of Cape Town; coalition majority in Nelson Mandela Bay; and conditional EFF support in Tshwane and Johannesburg. There is also potential for a DA win in Ekurhuleni, Nomura noted.

However, despite this seemingly guaranteed outcome, the lack of EFF commitment to any side puts everything “up in the air”, and puts South Africa in an awkward position in many key areas.

These are 5 realities South Africans need to face about the outcome of the local elections, and what they mean for the immediate future of the country:

1. The EFF has become vital

The EFF, a relatively new party on South Africa’s political landscape, has gone from a minority of radicals out of the 2014 national elections, to a vital component of South African politics in 2016.

The EFF emerged as the kingmaker in the local elections, wielding enough power to sway council votes in favour of the DA or the ANC. The party has publicly stated it would support parties in opposition to the ANC – but would deal with votes on a case-by-case basis.

“The EFF therefore remains incredibly important,” Attard Montalto said.

Nomura noted that the EFF’s decision to stay away from coalitions came as a surprise, and would likely upset much-needed stability in key economic hubs such as Tshwane and Johannesburg.

Coalition make-up

2. Local government could be chaos

With very few outright majorities coming from coalitions in hung municipalities across the country, governance is going to be unstable, if not chaotic.

“Somehow nothing seems certain,” Attard Montolto said. “For example the EFF is asking for a different mayoral candidate for Johannesburg than Herman Mashaba, who ran for the DA in the elections.”

“There is the issue of the AIC and the uncertainty over how the EFF will treat each vote and the budget act in council adds uncertainty. Then there is the issue of the EFF’s internal stability – that is even before we get to the minutiae of the workings and stability of the DA coalition.”

The analyst said that we would have to wait until after the first council meetings and the elections of mayors to get a better grasp of how things will go.

“Ultimately, the need for service delivery may bring all opposition parties together, including the EFF, but this seems a challenge.”

3. The results are not exactly investor-friendly

Attard Montalto said that the market is still overestimating the ‘good news story’ from the local elections.

“For example, a minority DA government in Johannesburg hamstrung by the EFF vote-by-vote jockeying is at significant risk of being less of an investor-friendly outcome than the investor-friendly ANC mayor Parks Tau outcome,” the analyst said.

Where there could be a potential ‘good news story’ is the DA providing more efficient government and service delivery in Nelson Mandela Bay – but that is only because the party has the coalition power to make solid decisions there.

In economic hubs like Tshwane and Johannesburg, the outcomes are still very much up in the air, which is not an environment investors like.

4. The ANC’s response to the loss will be damaging

“Markets are underestimating the chances of an ANC policy reaction to regain support, a reaction, which is directly correlated with the number of metros they lose,” the analyst said.

This response has already been seen taking place: soon after the election results were announced, the ANC executive moved to a 4-day meeting to discuss the outcome.

Coming out of the meeting were plans for the party to refocus its policies in a more populist direction – almost echoing the narrative of the EFF – specifically to restructure budgets to assist the poor and focus on job creation.

While these policies are nothing new, the big loss in the local election may push the ANC to pursue the populist route more aggressively – something ratings agencies earlier in the year warned the party against doing, as it would cost the economy dearly.

A more populist ANC still in power nationally, could have a more damaging outcome for the economy, and is one of the elements Nomura projects will send the rand to R17 to the dollar by year end.

5. Things aren’t going to change for a while

While the election results dawned a new, complicated period of politics for South Africa, the ANC remains very much in power, has rallied behind president Jacob Zuma, and looks set to follow its political path into 2017.

Nomura noted post-elections that Zuma has shown he is in control of the party, and would likely stay as president to 2018 before his preferred successor takes over.

“Fundamentally, we think markets are overestimating the chances of the ANC losing power nationally and in Gauteng in 2019 under a new ANC leader,” Attard Montalto said.

“As we published after the elections the status quo is here for some significant time to come, and may turn out to be more messy than expected.”

Press Release:


Mayors Muscle In
Will they deliver? That’s the question on voters’ mind this week. Carte Blanche meets Johannesburg’s Herman Mashaba and Tshwane’s Solly Msimanga, two of eight new mayors to this week take over the reins of the country’s key metros. How have political alliances and coalitions shaped the way in which the dust of recent municipal elections will settle?



Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: The African National Congress took a political beating in the 2016 local municipal elections – losing four of the major metros – Cape Town, Nelson Mandela Bay, Tshwane and Johannesburg are no longer under ANC rule.

AUBREY: Jacob Zuma is a big factor. He caused collateral damage to the image of the ANC.
MALULEKE: Even if the DA had no strategy, the ANC gave them a strategy through their own ineptness.

LINK: The real winner is the EFF – they are the kingmakers – they will make or break the visions of political parties who are dependent on them for their votes. LINK 5

UPSOUND JULIUS…. DA Must know us voting for them in these metro does not mean that we are in the bed together – they are a better devil.

AUBREY: They are hugging but they are not kissing

VO: Political analyst Aubrey Matshiqi says it’s going to be very hard to fake sincerity around ideological differences.

AUBREY: the EFF is definitely not an ally of the DA and I think ideology is a big matter despite what I say about politics being the art of the possible. NT1 M19

VO: While there is no outright single party winner and the ANC still holds a national majority, these are the metros matter says Professor Tinyinko Maluleke.

MALULEKE: I think that a loss at the local level in some ways is more costly in the long term – because if the EFF and Da were to do better – people will know it.

VO: The capital Tshwane & the country’s economic hub, Johannesburg now have two Democratic Alliance Mayors at the helm – they have promised change, but can they deliver?

Tshwane’s new boss is Solly Msimanga, 36 years old. A Corporate Executive, who worked his way up the political ranks – his plan is to bring accountability back to the city. Additional skills: He also makes a mean curry.

SOLLY: I think I’m bringing a level of corporate ethos – in government people float – not my money, not my time as long as I get time. INT2 M8

VO: The man in charge in Johannesburg, is Herman Mashaba, 57 years old. An Entrepreneur & self-proclaimed capitalist, yet a political Rookie – he aims to be the jobs-mayor. Additional skills: He’s quite the pianist.

HERMAN: // I grew up aspiring to the freemarket capitalist world because this is the world that can grow the economy – that can get us to fly and employ people and pay taxes. INt1 M10

VO: Both these men see a career in politics as a calling.

SOLLY: I’m not gonna see change if I continue living in this luxury house… this, to make this a country that my child can be proud of. INT2 M6
HERMAN: I didn’t go in to politics for any other reason than being concerned about my country. INT1 M2 // I blame Jacob Zuma for this – because if we had a responsive responsible government I won’t be sitting here. INT2 M2

VO: Political analysts have their reservations about the new men in charge.

AUBREY: I argued when Herman Mashaba was announced as the mayoral candidate for the DA that the DA was not serious about winning JHB// I do think he may become a liability to the DA along the way// INT1 M25
MALULEKE: Care will need to be taken that his political naivety doesn’t get in the way of his business plans and his almost blind faith in capitalism doesn’t blind him to social needs of the people INT2 M5

VO: There seems to be more faith in the man at the helm of the country’s capital city, Solly Msimanga.

AUBREY: I think he is a decent choice as mayor there is a major constraint - the policy framework of his party. INT1 M24
MALULEKE: he’s probably one to watch for the future – but does he have what it takes to run a metro such a Tshwane? We will have to wait and see. INT1 M32

VO: The mayors are determined to prove critics wrong and deliver a better future for South Africans.

The plan for the capital city, TSHWANE, is:
- To promote industrial business in the city by offering investors rates and tax incentives.
- And then to build the infrastructure needed for service delivery.

SOLLY: We want to make sure that we are speeding up the provisions of water, electricity….title deeds.

VO: He will demand accountability across the board.

SOLLY: We can not afford projects that are going over budget, we cannot allowed over limit – we need to accountable.

VO: Solly believes one the first steps is forcing government VIPs, to be more responsible, by banning blue light brigades from the capital - with the exception of the President’s convoy.

SOLLY: Why should we risk the lives of people – they should manage their time better…. INT4 M2




VO: Back in the country’s economic hub, Johannesburg, the plan is turn it into an investment city, attracting local and international investors, that will help boost taxes to build infrastructure.

Herman also plans to address e-Tolls from the city’s perspective.

HERMAN: if SANRAL wants it do it themselves, Are people are not safe – and we have the JMPD to protect our citizens // not to chase people that are not criminals.

VO: He’s determined put an end to connected people, benefitting from contracts.

HERMAN: you must put in the right people for the interest of the public – not because you know me – but you’re qualified and doing it for your country. INT2 M21

VO: And the same approach applies to the members of the two mayoral committees selected from the councillor bases and announced on Friday.

HERMAN: I have taken people that have the will to do things, and the ability to do – they have everything that the city requires INT3 M3

VO: Ten mayoral committee members made up of academics and activists - will take Johannesburg, the centre of business, into the next few years – 2 from the Inkata Freedom Party, the balance, DA councillors.

DEVI: HOW WILL YOUR MAYORAL COMMITTEE BE DIFFERENT?
SOLLY: We are bringing in people who have management skills, it’s important to me INT3 M8

VO: In the capital city, Solly claims his committee is the most diverse any Tshwane council has ever had - also featuring 8 DA councillors along with one from the African Christian Democratic Party and another from the Freedom Front Plus.

The stage has been set…For the first time since 1994, parties have been forced to collaborate and form coalitions to unlock hung municipalities – this, is new territory for our young democracy.

MALULEKE: It’s not going to be polite, it’s going to be very messy
AUBERY: there will be deadlock – there is even the possibility of collapse // INT1 M21

VO: But Solly hopes to get buy in from all parties, in effort, to do right by citizens.

SOLLY: We are not always going to use votes – this is what is for the good of the people. // INT4 M5

MALULEKE: When it works it will work because they share a common enemy – both of them just don’t want to see the ANC back in power –that is such a powerful incentive for them to work together. INT1 M23

VO: But if there is deliberate opposition – Solly says they will be called out – because the mission is clear.

SOLLY: If people want to block delivery – this is what is being block – if you are not getting 1,2 ,3 – this is why… INT4 M6

MALULEKE: I think whatever the politics, whatever the shenanigans – they have to keep their eyes on the ball.
AUBREY: // the South African voter is no longer prepared to be taken for granted. Any party whether it is the EFF or the ANC or the DA – will be removed by voters from power. INT1 M26




PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: Coalition councils are changing the political landscape in South Africa with political parties forced to collaborate and cooperate to avoid chaos.

PROMO 2
VO: A new era of political alliances and coalitions shape the future of municipal governance.

MALULEKE: When it works it will work because they share a common enemy – both of them just don’t want to see the ANC back in power
PROMO 3
VO: Hung municipalities will be unlocked by coalitions and alliances – changing the face of politics in SA..

SOLLY: We are not always going to use votes – this is what is for the good of the people. // INT4 M5

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): what does the future hold for SA with coalition governments taking control in 4 of the country's major cities?
metadata.Summary: While the ANC is still the country's ruling party - they've lost power in 4 of the 6 major cities in SA - with Tshwane & Johannesburg falling under two DA mayors. What does the mean for the country? How will these coalitions work? And these two new mayor's the right candidates - they promise change - but how will it be delivered?
metadata.Further information: South Africans are overestimating the “good news” of the DA, EFF and smaller parties ganging up against the ANC, as the political and economic realities in South Africa have just become far more complex. This is according to Nomura chief strategist for Africa, Peter Attard Montalto, who has provided a breakdown of the coalitions formed over the past few days, and a number of implications for investors looking to put money into the country. Coming out of the coalition talks, The DA looks set to gain mayorship and a degree of control in major metros in the country – metros which control 85% of the municipal finance budget in South Africa. This includes outright control of the City of Cape Town; coalition majority in Nelson Mandela Bay; and conditional EFF support in Tshwane and Johannesburg. There is also potential for a DA win in Ekurhuleni, Nomura noted. However, despite this seemingly guaranteed outcome, the lack of EFF commitment to any side puts everything “up in the air”, and puts South Africa in an awkward position in many key areas. These are 5 realities South Africans need to face about the outcome of the local elections, and what they mean for the immediate future of the country: 1. The EFF has become vital The EFF, a relatively new party on South Africa’s political landscape, has gone from a minority of radicals out of the 2014 national elections, to a vital component of South African politics in 2016. The EFF emerged as the kingmaker in the local elections, wielding enough power to sway council votes in favour of the DA or the ANC. The party has publicly stated it would support parties in opposition to the ANC – but would deal with votes on a case-by-case basis. “The EFF therefore remains incredibly important,” Attard Montalto said. Nomura noted that the EFF’s decision to stay away from coalitions came as a surprise, and would likely upset much-needed stability in key economic hubs such as Tshwane and Johannesburg. Coalition make-up 2. Local government could be chaos With very few outright majorities coming from coalitions in hung municipalities across the country, governance is going to be unstable, if not chaotic. “Somehow nothing seems certain,” Attard Montolto said. “For example the EFF is asking for a different mayoral candidate for Johannesburg than Herman Mashaba, who ran for the DA in the elections.” “There is the issue of the AIC and the uncertainty over how the EFF will treat each vote and the budget act in council adds uncertainty. Then there is the issue of the EFF’s internal stability – that is even before we get to the minutiae of the workings and stability of the DA coalition.” The analyst said that we would have to wait until after the first council meetings and the elections of mayors to get a better grasp of how things will go. “Ultimately, the need for service delivery may bring all opposition parties together, including the EFF, but this seems a challenge.” 3. The results are not exactly investor-friendly Attard Montalto said that the market is still overestimating the ‘good news story’ from the local elections. “For example, a minority DA government in Johannesburg hamstrung by the EFF vote-by-vote jockeying is at significant risk of being less of an investor-friendly outcome than the investor-friendly ANC mayor Parks Tau outcome,” the analyst said. Where there could be a potential ‘good news story’ is the DA providing more efficient government and service delivery in Nelson Mandela Bay – but that is only because the party has the coalition power to make solid decisions there. In economic hubs like Tshwane and Johannesburg, the outcomes are still very much up in the air, which is not an environment investors like. 4. The ANC’s response to the loss will be damaging “Markets are underestimating the chances of an ANC policy reaction to regain support, a reaction, which is directly correlated with the number of metros they lose,” the analyst said. This response has already been seen taking place: soon after the election results were announced, the ANC executive moved to a 4-day meeting to discuss the outcome. Coming out of the meeting were plans for the party to refocus its policies in a more populist direction – almost echoing the narrative of the EFF – specifically to restructure budgets to assist the poor and focus on job creation. While these policies are nothing new, the big loss in the local election may push the ANC to pursue the populist route more aggressively – something ratings agencies earlier in the year warned the party against doing, as it would cost the economy dearly. A more populist ANC still in power nationally, could have a more damaging outcome for the economy, and is one of the elements Nomura projects will send the rand to R17 to the dollar by year end. 5. Things aren’t going to change for a while While the election results dawned a new, complicated period of politics for South Africa, the ANC remains very much in power, has rallied behind president Jacob Zuma, and looks set to follow its political path into 2017. Nomura noted post-elections that Zuma has shown he is in control of the party, and would likely stay as president to 2018 before his preferred successor takes over. “Fundamentally, we think markets are overestimating the chances of the ANC losing power nationally and in Gauteng in 2019 under a new ANC leader,” Attard Montalto said. “As we published after the elections the status quo is here for some significant time to come, and may turn out to be more messy than expected.”
